extracted.intended_audience: students of commutative algebra (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-notes-style exposition of commutative algebra covering prime/maximal ideals, radicals, local rings, modules, and exact sequences; aimed at learning and doing exercises in these topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal ideals are prime
rubrics_metrics.description: In a ring, every maximal ideal is prime (Corollary (2.22)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that a field is a domain (2.3) and references results (2.9) and (2.17). The text gives a short proof: quotient by a maximal ideal is a field, hence a domain, so the ideal is prime.

rubrics_metrics.name: PID definition and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A domain R is a Principal Ideal Domain (PID) if every ideal is principal. Examples: k[X] for a field k; Z. Every PID is a UFD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of prime ideals in R[X] for PID R
rubrics_metrics.description: Let R be a PID and P = R[X]. For a prime ideal p of P: (1) p = <0>, or p = <f> with f prime, or p is maximal. (2) If p is maximal then either p = <f> with f prime, or p = <p0, g> with p0 a prime of R and g whose image g' in (R/<p0>)[X] is prime (Theorem (2.26)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses prime factorization, Gauss’s Lemma, passing to fraction field K and reduction mod a prime p0 in R; shows how primes either come from polynomials or lie over primes in R. Examples and exercises follow to test edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element is unit iff it belongs to no maximal ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: For x in R, x is a unit iff x belongs to no maximal ideal (Corollary (2.29)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the equivalence between ⟨x⟩ being the whole ring and x not being in any maximal ideal; relies on existence of maximal ideals (2.28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobson radical (rad(R))
rubrics_metrics.description: rad(R) is defined as the intersection of all maximal ideals of R (Definition (3.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the default 'radical' notion for nilpotence-related criteria; later characterized by equivalent statements (Proposition (3.2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of Jacobson radical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: x ∈ rad(R) iff 1 − x y is a unit for all y ∈ R (Proposition (3.2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if x lies in every maximal ideal m then 1−xy cannot lie in any m (otherwise contradiction), so 1−xy is a unit. Conversely, if x ∉ rad(R) pick maximal m not containing x and produce y with 1−xy ∉ U(R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local ring definition and Nonunit Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring A is local if it has exactly one maximal ideal. Lemma (3.4): A is local iff the set of nonunits n is an ideal; if so n is the unique maximal ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if n is an ideal it is proper and hence maximal; conversely in a local ring the set of nonunits equals the unique maximal ideal. Several examples (power series rings) illustrate the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal power series ring local property
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is local with maximal ideal m, then P = R[[X1,...,Xn]] is local with maximal ideal a + mP where a = ⟨X1,...,Xn⟩; nonunits are exactly a + mP (Example (3.7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given f ∉ maximal ideal can be written a(1−g) with a a unit and g ∈ a, then inverses are constructed by geometric-type series; shows canonical surjection P → R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of prime ideals disjoint from multiplicative set
rubrics_metrics.description: Let R a ring, S a multiplicative subset, and a an ideal with a ∩ S = ∅. The set of ideals disjoint from S and containing a has a maximal element p, and every such maximal p is prime (Proposition (3.9)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Zorn’s lemma: Zorn gives a maximal ideal p disjoint from S; primeness proven by standard argument expanding p with x or y and using multiplicativity to force contradiction if xy ∈ p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturated multiplicative subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: S ⊆ R multiplicative is saturated if xy ∈ S implies x,y ∈ S. Units form a saturated multiplicative subset. If φ: R→R' and T ⊆ R' saturated multiplicative then φ^{-1}(T) is saturated; converse holds if φ surjective (3.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saturation operation: S̄ = {x | ∃y with xy ∈ S}; R  ar{S} is union of primes disjoint from S (Exercise (3.14)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime Avoidance Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a be an additive-and-multiplicative-stable subset and p1,...,pn ideals with p3,...,pn prime. If a ⊄ ∪ pj then there exists x ∈ a with x ∉ pj for all j; equivalently if a ⊆ ∪_{i=1}^n p_i then a ⊆ p_i for some i (Lemma (3.15)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on n, standard construction of elements xi avoiding all but one prime and combining them. Exercises illustrate vector-space analogue over infinite fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of radical of an ideal (√a)
rubrics_metrics.description: √a := { x ∈ R | x^n ∈ a for some n ≥ 1 } (3.18). Radical of ideal equals intersection of all prime ideals containing a when a is intersection of primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: nilradical = √⟨0⟩; ring reduced iff nilradical = 0. Exercises ask to compute nilpotents in Z/⟨n⟩.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheinnullstellensatz (Radical equals intersection of primes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any ideal a of R, √a = ∩_{p ⊇ a} p, the intersection taken over all prime ideals containing a (Theorem (3.22)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs multiplicative set S = {1,x,x^2,...} to separate element x ∉ ∩ p and invoke (3.9) to find prime not containing x; the other inclusion is straightforward. Convention: empty intersection = R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical of an ideal is an ideal and closure properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The radical √a is an ideal; in particular √a = ∩_{p ⊇ a} p (Proposition (3.24)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof shows closure under addition via binomial-type expansion: if x^n ∈ a and y^m ∈ a then (x + y)^{m+n-1} ∈ a by summand argument. Also √(∩ a_i) = ∩ √a_i, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal primes and reduced rings imply domain
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is reduced with exactly one minimal prime q then R is a domain and q = ⟨0⟩ (Proposition (3.27)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: since ⟨0⟩ = ∩ primes and each prime contains q by minimality, intersection equals q, hence ⟨0⟩ = q and no zero divisors beyond 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module axioms and submodules
rubrics_metrics.description: An R-module M is an abelian group with scalar multiplication satisfying distributivity, associativity, and 1·m = m. Submodules are additive subgroups closed under scalar multiplication (4.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: over a field modules = vector spaces; Z-modules = abelian groups. Annihilators Ann(m) and Ann(M) are ideals; aN denotes submodule generated by products an.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module homomorphisms, kernel and image
rubrics_metrics.description: A homomorphism φ: M→N is R-linear. Ker(φ) and Im(φ) are submodules; Hom_R(M,N) is an R-module (4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard properties: φ is iso iff bijective; Hom has addition and scalar multiplication given pointwise; composition induces maps on Hom-sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endomorphism ring and multiplication-by-x map
rubrics_metrics.description: End_R(M) is a (possibly noncommutative) ring under composition. The map (·)_x : M→M given by m↦xm defines a ring hom R→End_R(M) with kernel Ann(M) (4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faithful module means the representation R→End_R(M) is injective (Ann(M)=0). Conversely a ring hom to End_Z(N) gives M the structure of an R-module.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of scalars and algebra structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Given R→R' making R' an R-algebra, any R'-module is an R-module by restriction of scalars. Conversely an R-module structure on R' with (xy)z = x(yz) yields an R-algebra structure on R' (4.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for compatibility with R'=R/a: an R-module M has a compatible R'-module structure iff aM=0; uniqueness follows. Subalgebra generation R[x1,...,xn] consists of polynomial combinations with coefficients in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue (quotient) module and its universal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Given submodule M' ⊆ M, the quotient M/M' with canonical map π: M→M/M' is the residue module; π is surjective with kernel M'. Universal mapping property: any φ: M→N vanishing on M' factors uniquely through π (4.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this UMP to identify quotients, factor maps, and prove Noether isomorphisms. In practice one often works with another module M'' equipped with a surjection from M having kernel M'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclic modules and annihilator correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: A module M is cyclic if M = R m for some m; then M ≅ R/Ann(m) (4.7). Conversely R/a is cyclic generated by coset of 1 and Ann(R/a) = a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives canonical identification and tests for cyclicity via existence of single generator and computation of annihilator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noether isomorphisms (First/Second/Third)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard isomorphisms: (1) N/(L) ≅ (N/L)/(M/L) etc. First, Second, and Third Isomorphism Theorems for modules are stated in (4.8) with canonical quotient maps and identifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally: when L⊆M⊆N, (N/L)/(M/L) ≅ N/M. For L+M and L∩M the usual isomorphisms hold. These are proved by factoring quotient maps and using UMP of quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cokernel and coimage; coimage ≅ image
rubrics_metrics.description: For φ: M→N, Coker(φ) := N/Im(φ) and Coim(φ) := M/Ker(φ). There is a canonical surjection Coim(φ) → Im(φ) and Coim(φ) ≅ Im(φ) (4.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cokernel has UMP: maps N→P that kill Im(φ) factor uniquely through Coker(φ). Use (4.6.1) to identify Coim with Im.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free modules and their universal property
rubrics_metrics.description: R^{(I)} (restricted functions with finite support) is free with standard basis e_i. A module is free of rank ℓ iff isomorphic to R^ℓ. UMP: given elements m_i in M indexed by I there is a unique map from R^{(I)} sending e_i↦m_i; injectivity/surjectivity criteria correspond to independence/generation (4.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Q as a Z-module is not free nor finitely generated. Free modules are characterized by existence of a basis and universal mapping property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct sums/products and Hom adjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct product ∏ M_i and direct sum ⊕ M_i have the usual UMPs. Hom(N,∏ M_i) ≅ ∏ Hom(N,M_i) and Hom(⊕ M_i, N) ≅ ∏ Hom(M_i, N) (4.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projections and injections realize the universal properties; finite-generation hypotheses produce isomorphisms in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact sequence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence ...→ M_{i} → M_{i+1} → ... is exact at M_i if Ker(next) = Im(prev). The sequence is exact if exact at every term except possibly initial source or final target (5.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short exact sequences 0→L→M→N→0 are exact iff L ≅ Ker and N ≅ Coker; many concrete tests and examples provided in (5.2),(5.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short exact sequences and split exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: A short exact sequence 0→M'→M→M''→0 splits iff M ≅ M' ⊕ M'' (5.8). Equivalent conditions: existence of retraction M→M' (left inverse) or section M''→M (right inverse) (Proposition (5.9)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive consequences: if a section exists, one obtains explicit decomposition; if a retraction exists, one can produce a section and vice versa. Exercises ask to critique misstatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness preserved by products and sums
rubrics_metrics.description: If sequences indexed by i are exact, then the direct sum and direct product of those sequences are exact; conversely exactness of the induced product or sum sequences implies exactness of each component (Proposition (5.4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is immediate from componentwise definition of kernels and images and from universal properties of direct sums/products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snake Lemma and induced long exact sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a commutative diagram with exact rows (5.12), the Snake Lemma produces a connecting morphism @ and an exact sequence connecting kernels and cokernels: Ker(α') → Ker(α) → Ker(α'') →^{@} Coker(α') → Coker(α) → Coker(α'') (Lemma (5.12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma constructs all maps except @ canonically and then defines @ to complete exactness; additional remarks: if certain maps are injective/surjective then corresponding induced maps inherit injectivity/surjectivity.
